sections.title: Before starting
sections.text: Confirm the mutation, treatment setting, prescription, baseline tests, first review and emergency contact.

sections.title: Taking the tablets
sections.text: Take at the same time daily without food: leave at least 3 hours after food before the dose and wait at least 1 hour afterwards before eating. Swallow with water. If missed, take it the same day unless the next dose is due within 8 hours; then skip. Never double a dose or repeat a vomited dose. Ask pharmacy for the approved water-dispersion method if swallowing is difficult.

sections.title: Supplies and visits
sections.text: Arrange the next prescription before tablets run out. Keep your blood-test and clinic appointments. The oral regimen itself does not require an infusion line or pump.

sections.title: If treatment is held
sections.text: Ask why, what must recover and when review is due. Only the team authorises restarting or changing dose.

sections.title: At treatment change
sections.text: Agree ongoing symptom care, scans, contraception and follow-up.

evidence.title: Evidence for this treatment setting
evidence.intro: The mutation and prior treatment matter.
evidence.interpretation: In studies of selected EGFR-mutated advanced lung cancers, afatinib delayed cancer progression compared with cisplatin/pemetrexed. The overall survival comparison in that trial was not statistically significant. A separate comparison with gefitinib also did not show a statistically significant overall-survival difference. Ask how the study population and alternatives match your situation.
evidence.limitations: Study groups cannot predict your individual outcome or compare treatments from different trials.

patient.teachback: Can you explain how to take your tablets, what to do after a missed or vomited dose, which tests are next and which symptoms mean you should call today?
patient.consent_support: Discuss the aim of advanced cancer control, expected benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including not proceeding, bowel and skin effects, serious lung/liver problems, fertility and pregnancy, daily treatment, monitoring and your right to reconsider.

support.title: Diarrhoea and fluids
support.text: Keep prescribed anti-diarrhoea medicine available from the first dose. Start your agreed plan at the first loose stool, keep drinking if able and report symptoms early. Your team may advise continuing symptom medicine until loose stools have stopped for 12 hours. Severe diarrhoea, weakness or reduced urine needs urgent advice.

support.title: Skin, nails and mouth
support.text: Use the agreed EGFR-inhibitor skin-care and mouth-care plan. Emollients and sun protection may help; report rash, painful nails or mouth sores early. The team decides whether creams, antibiotics or other treatment are needed.

support.title: Nausea medicines
support.text: Afatinib has minimal-to-low oral emetic risk. Routine infusion premedication is not required. Agree any as-needed anti-sickness medicine with the team, after checking interactions and your medical history.

support.title: Medicine interactions
support.text: Give pharmacy a list of all medicines, herbal products and supplements. Some P-gp inhibitors need separated dosing; strong inducers such as St John’s wort can reduce afatinib exposure. Ask for a written individual schedule before adding or changing medicines.

support.title: Pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding
support.text: Avoid pregnancy. Women who could become pregnant need adequate contraception during treatment and for at least 1 month after the final dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Discuss fertility and future pregnancy plans before starting.

questions.q: Is there a planned week off?
questions.a: No. These tablets are continuous daily treatment. A hold for side effects is a clinical decision.

questions.q: What if I miss a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Take at the same time daily without food: leave at least 3 hours after food before the dose and wait at least 1 hour afterwards before eating. Swallow with water. If missed, take it the same day unless the next dose is due within 8 hours; then skip. Never double a dose or repeat a vomited dose. questions.q: Can I adjust the dose myself?
questions.a: No. Keep the prescription and contact plan. Your team authorises every hold, restart or dose change.

questions.q: Do I need all the tests every day?

clinical.component_rationale: Afatinib is an irreversible EGFR-family tyrosine kinase inhibitor. It interrupts signals involved in cancer-cell growth; the tumour mutation test and treatment setting determine whether it is suitable.
key_points: Keep EGFR-TKI-naïve NCCP scope separate from licensed squamous post-platinum disease.
Grade 2 diarrhoea >48 hours or rash >7 days, intolerable grade 2, or grade ≥3: hold until grade 0/1, then discuss a 10 mg reduction.
Suspected ILD: hold and investigate; confirmed ILD: permanently stop. Pre-existing ILD is an NCCP exclusion.
NCCP CrCl <15/dialysis and Child–Pugh C recommendations conflict with EMA restrictions; no automatic dose is supplied.
NCCP monthly blood tests and indication-based LVEF assessment; daily drug schedule is not a 28-day cycle.

patient_selection.treatment_intent: Control advanced disease and delay progression; no fixed course cap.
disease_and_biomarker_context: NCCP 00221a covers adults with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with an activating EGFR mutation who have not received an EGFR TKI. The separate licensed squamous-cancer indication after platinum treatment is not included in this NCCP regimen or its evidence card.
eligibility_orientation: NCCP 00221a: adult EGFR-TKI-naïve activating-EGFR locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC.
Validated activating EGFR test. NCCP v5 has no numerical ECOG cutoff.
important_cautions: NCCP CrCl-based no-adjustment-expected at <15/dialysis vs EMA indexed-eGFR <15/dialysis treatment not recommended.
NCCP Child–Pugh C no adjustment expected vs EMA not recommended.
NCCP and EMA do not specify CTCAE edition in the afatinib dose table.
LUX-Lung 3 randomised 345 previously untreated patients with EGFR-mutated stage IIIB/IV lung adenocarcinoma to afatinib or cisplatin/pemetrexed. This is advanced disease, not adjuvant therapy.
The LUX-Lung 3 overall-population OS comparison was not statistically significant. Exon-19 deletion subgroup OS findings must not be applied to every EGFR mutation.

LUX-Lung 7 compared afatinib with gefitinib in common Ex19del/L858R mutations. Its mature OS comparison was not statistically significant. It is not a comparison against current third-generation EGFR therapy.
The licensed post-platinum squamous indication and LUX-Lung 8 evidence are outside NCCP 00221a. Trial groups do not predict an individual outcome.

clinical.support_summary: Minimal-to-low oral emetic risk; no routine parenteral premedication. Individual as-required antiemetics, early diarrhoea support, skin/mouth care, hydration and medicine reconciliation.
baseline: LVEF by ECHO/MUGA if clinically indicated.
before_each_cycle: Continuous daily treatment has no invented cycle. At each planned review confirm adherence, toxicity, hydration, medicine changes, investigations and supply.
ongoing: FBC, renal and liver profile monthly.

If unable to swallow, pharmacy may teach the approved non-carbonated-water dispersion method; do not crush.
access: Oral treatment; no infusion line or ambulatory pump for this monotherapy. Pharmacy review and tablet supply remain essential.

rationale.summary: Afatinib blocks abnormal EGFR-family growth signals in selected lung cancers. Treatment aims to control advanced cancer and delay progression.
factors: Validated activating EGFR mutation, exact prior treatments, performance status, organ function, medicine interactions and patient priorities.
alternatives: Discuss current MDT-approved systemic options, clinical trials and supportive care, including not proceeding, for the exact mutation and setting.
limitations: LUX-Lung 3 randomised 345 previously untreated patients with EGFR-mutated stage IIIB/IV lung adenocarcinoma to afatinib or cisplatin/pemetrexed. This is advanced disease, not adjuvant therapy.
The LUX-Lung 3 overall-population OS comparison was not statistically significant. Exon-19 deletion subgroup OS findings must not be applied to every EGFR mutation.

LUX-Lung 7 compared afatinib with gefitinib in common Ex19del/L858R mutations. Its mature OS comparison was not statistically significant. It is not a comparison against current third-generation EGFR therapy.
The licensed post-platinum squamous indication and LUX-Lung 8 evidence are outside NCCP 00221a. Trial groups do not predict an individual outcome.

sections.text: Arrange the next prescription before tablets run out. Keep your blood-test and clinic appointments. The oral regimen itself does not require an infusion line or pump.

sections.title: If treatment is held
sections.text: Ask why, what must recover and when review is due. Only the team authorises restarting or changing dose.

sections.title: At treatment change
sections.text: Agree ongoing symptom care, scans, contraception and follow-up.

evidence.title: Evidence for this treatment setting
evidence.intro: The mutation and prior treatment matter.
evidence.interpretation: In a study of previously untreated advanced lung cancer with common EGFR mutations, dacomitinib delayed progression and improved overall survival compared with gefitinib. The study excluded people with a history of brain or other central nervous system metastases. It did not compare dacomitinib with every treatment available today. Group results cannot predict your own outcome.
evidence.limitations: Study groups cannot predict your individual outcome or compare treatments from different trials.

patient.teachback: Can you explain how to take your tablets, what to do after a missed or vomited dose, which tests are next and which symptoms mean you should call today?
patient.consent_support: Discuss the aim of advanced cancer control, expected benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including not proceeding, bowel and skin effects, serious lung/liver problems, fertility and pregnancy, daily treatment, monitoring and your right to reconsider.

support.title: Diarrhoea and fluids
support.text: Keep prescribed anti-diarrhoea medicine available from the first dose. Start your agreed plan at the first loose stool, keep drinking if able and report symptoms early. Your team may advise continuing symptom medicine until loose stools have stopped for 12 hours. Severe diarrhoea, weakness or reduced urine needs urgent advice.

support.title: Skin, nails and mouth
support.text: Use the agreed EGFR-inhibitor skin-care and mouth-care plan. Emollients and sun protection may help; report rash, painful nails or mouth sores early. The team decides whether creams, antibiotics or other treatment are needed.

support.title: Nausea medicines
support.text: Dacomitinib has minimal-to-low oral emetic risk. Routine infusion premedication is not required. Agree any as-needed anti-sickness medicine with the team, after checking interactions and your medical history.

support.title: Medicine interactions
support.text: Acid-suppressing medicines can reduce dacomitinib exposure. Proton pump inhibitors should be avoided if possible; ask pharmacy about alternatives. NCCP and current product information give different timing before H2 blockers, so obtain a written individual schedule. CYP2D6 medicines also need pharmacy review. Do not change medicines yourself.

support.title: Pregnancy, fertility and breastfeeding
support.text: Avoid pregnancy. Women who could become pregnant need adequate contraception during treatment and for at least 17 days after the final dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment. Discuss fertility and future pregnancy plans before starting.

endocrine_timeline.title: Daily tablets, checks and decisions
endocrine_timeline.intro: No dates or personal information are needed. Confirm your own appointments with the team.

rows.label: Preparation
rows.text: Confirm the activating EGFR test, indication, prescription and baseline tests.

rows.label: Daily oral treatment
rows.text: The usual starting dose is 45 mg by mouth once daily, continuously without a planned rest week. Use the dose on your prescription; some patients start lower because of liver function. Treatment continues while it helps and side effects remain acceptable.

rows.label: Tests and symptoms
rows.text: NCCP requires regular blood count, kidney, liver and bone tests but does not specify a fixed interval; your team sets appointments. Diarrhoea often starts early, so keep the symptom plan ready from the first dose. Scans follow your Consultant’s plan.

rows.label: Next treatment plan
rows.text: Review response, side effects and whether to continue, change or stop treatment.

questions.q: Is there a planned week off?
questions.a: No. These tablets are continuous daily treatment. A hold for side effects is a clinical decision.

questions.q: What if I miss a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Take at approximately the same time each day with or without food and swallow with water. If you miss a dose or vomit, do not take a replacement or extra dose. Take your next prescribed dose at the usual time the following day.

questions.q: Can I adjust the dose myself?
questions.a: No. Keep the prescription and contact plan. Your team authorises every hold, restart or dose change.

questions.q: Do I need all the tests every day?
questions.a: No. Your team schedules tests and reviews. Contact them between appointments if symptoms occur.

chapters.title: Your treatment aim
chapters.intro: Dacomitinib blocks abnormal EGFR-family growth signals in selected lung cancers. Treatment aims to control advanced cancer and delay progression.

chapters.title: When to get urgent help
chapters.intro: Do not wait for the next appointment.

items.title: Call urgently
items.text: Call urgently for new or worsening breathlessness, cough or fever; severe diarrhoea, inability to drink or much less urine; severe or peeling skin reactions; or yellow skin/eyes. Eye pain, light sensitivity or blurred vision needs prompt assessment. Severe breathing difficulty, collapse or swelling of the tongue/throat needs emergency help. Use your unit’s temperature and 24-hour contact instructions.

items.title: When you call
items.text: Give the medicine name, last dose and symptoms. Tell the team if you can drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Do not delay calling while gathering information.

chapters.title: What studies tell us
chapters.intro: In a study of previously untreated advanced lung cancer with common EGFR mutations, dacomitinib delayed progression and improved overall survival compared with gefitinib. The study excluded people with a history of brain or other central nervous system metastases. It did not compare dacomitinib with every treatment available today. Group results cannot predict your own outcome.

items.title: Your own decision
items.text: Ask how the study population matches your situation and discuss alternatives, harms and remaining uncertainty.

chapters.title: When treatment changes
chapters.intro: The team authorises continuation, interruption, restart or stopping.

items.title: Before restarting
items.text: Confirm symptom recovery, blood results, the prescribed dose and the next review.

items.title: When treatment ends
items.text: Agree follow-up, unresolved symptom care and reproductive precautions.

clinical.component_rationale: Dacomitinib is an irreversible EGFR-family tyrosine kinase inhibitor. It interrupts signals involved in cancer-cell growth; the tumour mutation test and treatment setting determine whether it is suitable.
key_points: First-line activating-EGFR advanced NSCLC; NCCP ECOG 0–1.

Grade 2 diarrhoea persisting 24 hours despite treatment or skin toxicity persisting 72 hours despite treatment requires a hold. After recovery to grade ≤1, same versus reduced dose is a Consultant choice.
Grade ≥3 diarrhoea/skin: hold to grade ≤1 then reduce one level; other grade ≥3 toxicity: hold to grade ≤2 then reduce one level.
Suspected ILD: hold during evaluation; confirmed ILD: permanently discontinue at any grade.
Severe hepatic start is 30 mg, with optional escalation after ≥4 weeks if tolerated; severe renal impairment/dialysis has no established recommendation.
H2-blocker timing differs between NCCP and EMA. Resolve with pharmacy; avoid PPIs and review CYP2D6 substrates.

patient_selection.treatment_intent: Control advanced disease and delay progression; no fixed course cap.
disease_and_biomarker_context: NCCP 00565a covers first-line treatment of adults with locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC with an activating EGFR mutation. This is daily dacomitinib alone; it is not an adjuvant regimen or a chemotherapy combination.
eligibility_orientation: NCCP 00565a: first-line adult activating-EGFR locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC.
Validated EGFR test; ECOG 0–1; adequate renal, hepatic and haematological status.
important_cautions: Known hypersensitivity to dacomitinib or excipients
H2-receptor antagonist timing: NCCP ≥6 hours before/10 hours after vs EMA 2 hours before/≥10 hours after. Requires pharmacy reconciliation.
NCCP v3 published review date 23 June 2026 has passed; retrieved current linked source remains v3, not a claim of independent reapproval.

ARCHER 1050 randomised 452 treatment-naïve adults with advanced EGFR Ex19del/L858R NSCLC and ECOG 0–1; patients with a history of CNS metastases were excluded. Do not generalise its results to CNS-metastatic or all uncommon EGFR-mutation populations.
The comparator was gefitinib, not osimertinib or a modern combination. No cross-trial superiority is claimed.
The extended OS analysis was ad hoc at a protocol-defined long-term cutoff. Dose-reduction subgroup outcomes are non-randomised and do not establish that reducing dose improves survival.
The regimen remains the current linked NCCP v3 document despite its listed June 2026 review date. Source retrieval is not independent clinical approval.

access: Oral treatment; no infusion line or ambulatory pump for this monotherapy. Pharmacy review and tablet supply remain essential.
